UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman; 
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See, 
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte. 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
 
ORDER ACCEPTING TARIFF REVISIONS IN PART  
AND REJECTING TARIFF REVISIONS IN PART 
 
(Issued October 9, 2026) 
 
1. 
On August 13, 2026, pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (FPA),1 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) submitted proposed revisions to its Open Access 
Transmission Tariff (OATT) and Reliability Assurance Agreement (RAA) (collectively, 
Tariff) to establish:  (1) a definition of Large Load; (2) a Large Load Registry; (3) a new 
Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS); (4) a requirement for Load Serving Entities 
(LSE) serving New Large Load to designate new capacity resources in an amount at least 
equal to the New Large Load’s peak load to avoid the New Large Load being subject to 
IRAS; (5) rules for Bring Your Own New Capacity (BYONC) arrangements; and (6) 
rules to exclude Eligible New Large Load from the Variable Resource Requirement 
(VRR) curve beginning with Delivery Year 2029/2030.   
2. 
In this order, we accept PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions to establish a definition of 
Large Load and a Large Load Registry, effective October 12, 2026, as requested, and 
require PJM to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the date of issuance of this 
order.  We reject PJM’s remaining proposed Tariff revisions, as discussed below. 
I. 
Filing Overview 
3. 
PJM states that, beginning in the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, it will be short of 
sufficient capacity to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement, particularly due to 
data center load growth and the pace of data center interconnection.2  PJM’s proposal to 
address this challenge includes several elements:  (1) a definition of Large Load; (2) a 
Large Load Registry, which is a database of information pertaining to Large Loads that

curtailments during periods when there are insufficient resources to reliably meet demand

new capacity resources in an amount at least equal to the New Large Load’s peak load; 
(5) rules for BYONC arrangements; and (6) rules to exclude Eligible New Large Load 
from the VRR curve beginning with Delivery Year 2029/2030.  PJM’s proposed Tariff 
revisions, as described further below, would implicate and assign responsibilities to 
several entities in PJM, including the Electric Distributor,3 the LSE,4 and the 
Transmission Owner.5 
4.

II. 
Notice of Filing and Responsive Pleadings 
5.

6.

7.

III. 
Discussion 
A. 
Procedural Matters 
9. 
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,        
18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the notices of intervention and timely, unopposed motions to 
intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding. 
10. 
Pursuant to Rule 214(d) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,     
18 C.F.R. § 385.214(d), we grant CyrusOne and Governor Shapiro’s late-filed motions to 
intervene given their interest in the proceeding, the early stage of the proceeding, and the 
absence of undue prejudice or delay.  We also accept the out-of-time comments and 
protests submitted by CyrusOne, Equinix, IECA, OPSI, PAG, Representative Pallone, the 
Virginia Commission, and Voltus. 
11. 
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. 
§ 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest or answer unless otherwise 
ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the answers filed by AEP, AEU, 
Buckeye, CEBA, Constellation, Data Center Coalition, EKPC, FirstEnergy, Google, 
Governor Shapiro, IMM, NJBPU, PJM, PPL, SMECO, Vistra, and Voltus because they 
have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process. 
B. 
Substantive Matters 
12. 
PJM’s proposal consists of several elements that, when combined, are intended to 
address the capacity shortfall that, absent the entrance of new capacity resources, will 
prevent PJM from satisfying the PJM Region Reliability Requirement starting in the 
2027/2028 Delivery Year.  The first element of PJM’s proposal is to establish definitions 
of Large Load and New Large Load.  The latter is designed to capture the Delivery Year 
when PJM’s capacity shortfall, which PJM contends is the result of data center load

growth,11 first emerges.  Next, PJM proposes to develop a Large Load Registry to foster 
transparency regarding Large Load additions.  With that foundation, PJM proposes to 
adopt the IRAS framework, under which LSEs that seek to use Network Integration 
Transmission Service (NITS)12 to serve New Large Loads must designate sufficient new 
capacity resources, referred to as BYONC, to serve the New Large Load.  If an LSE 
using NITS to serve New Large Load fails to designate sufficient capacity resources, 
such New Large Load will be “subject to load reduction requests” when there are 
insufficient resources to reliably meet demand in real-time operations.13  In essence, the 
requirement that these New Large Loads must curtail under certain emergency conditions 
is designed to allow PJM to address its capacity shortfall.14   
13. 
As outlined in greater detail below, we accept PJM’s proposal in part, effective 
October 12, 2026, as requested, reject PJM’s proposal in part, and direct PJM to submit a 
compliance filing within 30 days of the date of this order.15  Specifically, we accept 
PJM’s proposal to establish a definition for Large Load and a Large Load Registry.16  We 
find that those two elements of PJM’s proposal are just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory or preferential.  Given PJM’s consent to sever or modify its proposal, we 
do so here.  We find that the elements of PJM’s proposal to establish a new definition of 
Large Load and a Large Load Registry are severable from the remainder of the filing and 
therefore may be accepted even though we reject the remainder of the proposal.

14. 
While we recognize the imminent capacity shortfall in PJM, we find that two key 
aspects of PJM’s proposal—IRAS and BYONC—are either outside of the Commission’s 
authority or have not been sufficiently demonstrated to be just and reasonable and not 
unduly discriminatory or preferential.  We do not take this decision lightly.  But given the 
significant discrepancies between PJM’s transmittal letter description of its proposed 
IRAS framework and its proposed Tariff revisions, as well as the lack of justification for 
many aspects of IRAS and BYONC, we cannot find that these elements of PJM’s 
proposal are just and reasonable.  We therefore reject these elements of the proposal.  
However, we provide guidance on how PJM could modify its proposal should PJM seek 
to refile it. 
15. 
Moreover, because the elements of PJM’s proposal other than the Large Load 
definition and Large Load Registry represent an integrated package that must be viewed 
as a whole, we reject the remainder of PJM’s proposal.  PJM, while consenting to 
severance and modification of the proposal, acknowledges that the RAA and OATT 
revisions are “designed to work in lockstep and provide complementary pieces.”17  We 
find that the remaining elements of PJM’s proposal, such as the proposed rules for 
BYONC arrangements and the exclusion of Eligible New Large Loads from the VRR 
curve, are not simply complementary, but instead are inextricably linked.  For example, 
the new obligation for LSEs seeking to use NITS to serve New Large Load to bring new 
capacity to avoid curtailment under IRAS is foundational to both the IRAS and BYONC 
frameworks.  It also establishes the need for the rules for BYONC arrangements and 
facilitates excluding Eligible New Large Loads from the VRR curve.  As such, we 
conclude that, contrary to PJM’s statements in its transmittal, the only elements of its 
proposal that are severable are the proposed definition of Large Load and the proposed 
Large Load Registry, which can be implemented independent of the IRAS and BYONC 
frameworks. 
1. 
Large Load Definition and Registry 
a. 
Definition of Large Load   
i. 
PJM’s Proposal 
16. 
PJM proposes to define Large Load as:   
end-use customer(s) load that has a cumulative peak load of 
50 [MW] or greater at a single electrical site behind one or 
more points of interconnection, where for configurations 
involving multiple affiliated load facilities or multiple points 
of interconnection with affiliated load facilities behind them,

17. 
Acknowledging that the Commission recently stated that PJM may establish its 
own definition of large load,19 PJM states that its definition differs from the 
Commission’s preliminary definition in several ways, and that these differences reflect 
the characteristics and realities of Large Loads in the PJM Region.20  The differences 
include:  (1) setting a 50 MW cumulative peak threshold; (2) establishing a one-mile 
radius at a single electrical site for Large Loads interconnected at multiple points; (3) 
using the term “end-use customer(s) load” instead of “new, commercial or industrial 
customer;” (4) including co-located loads and loads with behind-the-meter generation; 
and (5) excluding a voltage threshold.21  PJM states that it proposes to define a Large 
Load as located at a single electrical site behind one or more points of interconnection 
within a one-mile radius to avoid a scenario where, for example, a data center owner is 
not categorized as Large Load simply because the owner has elected to site a number of 
smaller data centers, each with peak loads below 50 MW, close together.  PJM states that 
the Commission has explicitly adopted a one-mile test in other situations to determine 
whether facilities are “at the same site” to be a Qualifying Facility.

ii. 
Pleadings 
19. 
Protesters argue that PJM has not properly justified the 50 MW threshold for

MW threshold to 200 MW, or to limit the definition to new data centers, to avoid

20. 
Some protesters also assert that PJM’s distinction between new and existing Large

In its answer, PJM highlights the importance of timely Commission approval of 
the definition of Large Load.39  In response to arguments that the 50 MW threshold is 
unsupported and should be changed, PJM asserts that the 50 MW threshold is in keeping 
with what was contemplated by the Commission and that no information presented 
renders PJM’s proposed threshold unjust and unreasonable.40  Further, PJM contends 
that, since PJM has proposed that 50 MW is the appropriate threshold necessary for 
purposes of tracking Large Loads and ensuring PJM has visibility into them to ensure 
reliability, it would be contradictory to ignore any MW that may have existed as a Large 
Load before an additional 50 MW were added. 
23. 
In response to parties’ arguments that PJM should differentiate between data 
center Large Loads and other types of Large Loads (e.g., manufacturing or industrial 
loads), PJM asserts that it is implementing the approach the Commission set forth in the 
PJM Large Load Show Cause Order—i.e., treating data center and computational, 
manufacturing, industrial, or other types of large loads the same.  PJM argues that the 
parties have shown no basis for deviating from the Commission’s approach.41 
24. 
In its answer, Data Center Coalition argues the PJM’s one-mile rule is not just and 
reasonable.42  Data Center Coalition argues that the proposed one-mile rule would 
unfairly subject long-operating legacy facilities to IRAS and potential curtailment merely

already been accounted for through regional planning.43  Data Center Coalition also 
argues that PJM’s undefined use of “affiliated” to aggregate facilities within a one-mile 
radius could improperly treat independent facilities as a single Large Load; therefore, 
Data Center Coalition asserts, the term’s criteria and application should be clearly 
specified in the Tariff rather than deferred to the PJM Manuals.44  The IMM similarly 
argues that PJM has not provided clear, uniform criteria for applying the one-mile radius

iii. 
Determination 
27. 
We find that PJM’s proposed definition of Large Load is just and reasonable and 
not unduly discriminatory or preferential.49  First, we find that establishing the threshold 
to qualify as a Large Load at a cumulative peak of 50 MW strikes a just and reasonable 
balance between capturing the larger loads into which PJM needs visibility to ensure the 
reliability of its system and excluding smaller loads that do not raise the same reliability 
concerns in PJM.50  We acknowledge protesters’ arguments that PJM has not explained

28. 
In addition, we disagree with protesters’ arguments that the definition of Large 
Load should be modified to exclude manufacturing facilities and include only data 
centers.  Protesters do not appear to argue that other types of large loads do not use 
energy at the same magnitude as data centers or do not have the same potential impacts 
on the transmission system.  Nor do protesters appear to argue that other types of large 
loads otherwise have different effects on resource adequacy that would justify excluding 
them from the definition of Large Load.  As such, we find reasonable PJM’s proposal to 
include all types of large loads in the Large Load definition.   
29. 
We acknowledge that commenters put forth alternate definitions of Large Load in 
the record.  However, having found PJM’s proposed definition of Large Load just and 
reasonable, as discussed above, we need not opine on these alternate definitions.  For 
filings made under FPA section 205, the Commission evaluates whether the proposal in 
the filing is just and reasonable, and not whether alternative proposals are more or less 
reasonable than the filing party’s proposal.52 
30.

together and affiliated are considered as a single facility for the purposes of the Large 
Load definition.  We agree with PJM that this requirement will preclude a scenario 
where, for example, a data center load is not categorized as Large Load simply because

proposal, we encourage PJM to clearly identify the product or service IRAS is intended 
to provide and ensure its proposed Tariff revisions consistently reflect that 
characterization.  We also encourage PJM to consider providing a description of how it 
will transition from any proposed types of service back to its traditional market structures 
and how it will avoid a long-term bifurcation of loads in the PJM market.  Although we 
are rejecting PJM’s proposal, PJM may consider refiling an alternative proposal under 
FPA section 205 that considers the guidance provided herein. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The Commission orders: 
 
(A) 
PJM’s proposal is hereby accepted in part, effective October 12, 2026, as 
requested, and rejected in part, as discussed in the body of the order. 
(B) 
PJM is hereby directed to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the 
date of this order, as discussed in the body of this order.

ROSNER, Commissioner, concurring:  
 
1. 
I agree with the decision to reject the bulk of PJM’s filing for the reasons 
articulated in today’s order.  I write separately to emphasize that, if PJM chooses to refile 
its proposal, it must justify its proposal to curtail IRAS load on a mandatory basis before 
load that has voluntarily enrolled in a demand response program.  I also urge PJM to 
carefully consider the consequences any refiled proposal might have on its capacity 
market. 
2. 
Customers in a demand response program allow a utility to reduce their demand 
without resorting to the extreme measure of manually pulling breakers on the utility’s 
distribution network.  Demand response customers also receive payments in exchange for 
volunteering to reduce their usage when the grid is stressed.  This structure is designed to 
protect consumers and their equipment from the draconian measure of being involuntarily 
forced off the system, as well as to send efficient market signals based on actual system 
conditions. 
3. 
PJM’s filing flips this paradigm, proposing to force IRAS load off the system in 
the earliest stages of emergency conditions,1 before PJM deploys demand response.2   
4. 
Moreover, PJM’s proposal would force IRAS load off the system in lieu of 
sending capacity price signals that are needed to get new infrastructure built.  Because 
PJM would forcibly curtail IRAS load before other firm load, PJM excludes IRAS load 
from its capacity market demand curve.  The result could be a capacity market signaling 
that PJM has more than enough capacity while the region sheds thousands of megawatts 
of demand on an involuntary basis.  That’s not only economically inefficient, but also 
likely to prevent supply and demand from coming back into balance.   
 
1 That is, during a NERC EEA 1 event. 
2 PJM cleared 7,017 MW of demand response in its most recent capacity auction.  
See PJM, 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction Report, at 15 (Jul. 14, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2028-
2029/2028-2029-bra-results-report.pdf.

Docket No. ER26-3515-000  
- 2 - 
 
5. 
To be clear, in an emergency, data centers not serving critical functions should be 
shut off before ordinary customers (Hint: homes, hospitals, and schools should never be 
curtailed before data centers).  We need state regulators to establish clear rules for which 
customers should be curtailed first when circumstances require it.  And we need PJM to 
be ready to adjust their operations to this evolving paradigm.  But such measures should 
only be taken when necessary to keep the system reliable, after voluntary demand 
response resources have been exhausted.   
 
For these reasons, I respectfully concur.
